lesson.title: Reading data safely
lesson.subtitle: Hidden groups, fair claims, private pupils

video.title: Reading data safely: Hidden groups, fair claims, private pupils
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - the students' teacher (main character)
Ms Farah - the students' head teacher (cameo)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: A visitor told our school: the morning class does better than the afternoon class, so afternoon lessons should end. The averages agreed. But the averages were hiding something.
Today: how to read data claims carefully, and how to keep pupils' data private.
We looked inside the groups. The afternoon class had most of the pupils who joined this year, and many were still learning English. Within each group, the two classes scored about the same.
So the time of day was not the cause. Two things can go together without one causing the other. Before you act on a pattern, ask: what else could explain it?
Be careful with small groups too. A class of eight can swing a lot from one test to the next. One good or bad day changes the average. Look at several tests before you judge.
Now privacy. When I share results, I share the class picture, not a child. Marks, health and family details stay private. A ranked list on the wall can hurt a pupil for years.

scenes.on_screen_text: Hide names, keep only what you need
scenes.narration: Use pupil numbers instead of names. Collect only what your question needs. Keep the list of names locked away, and delete the data when you are done.
Quick check! Pupils who eat breakfast at school get better marks. Does that prove breakfast causes better marks?

Not on its own. Pupils who come early for breakfast may also miss fewer lessons, or live closer to school. Breakfast may well help, but the pattern alone does not prove it. A fair test would compare similar pupils.
In the app, open the bias lab. See how data that leaves out a group gives unfair answers, and how fixing the data changes them.
Your turn. You want to show parents how the class did in a test. What is the safest thing to share?
The class average and spread, not names. Remember: look inside the groups, ask what else could explain a pattern, and be careful with small groups. Share the class, never the child.
Try it yourself: find one claim with a number in an advert or a post. Ask what else could explain it, and what data would check it, before you share it.

checkpoints.prompt: Pupils who eat breakfast at school get better marks. Does that prove breakfast causes better marks?

options.text: Not on its own: something else may explain it

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: pupils who come early may also miss fewer lessons. A pattern alone is not proof.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: two things can go together without one causing the other. Ask what else could explain it.

checkpoints.prompt: What is the safest way to show parents how the class did?

options.text: A ranked list from best to worst

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: the class picture tells parents enough without pointing at any child.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: names and rankings expose children. Share the class average and spread.
